title: Web Search Engine
description: Design web search — building a sharded inverted index from crawled pages, query serving with scatter-gather, ranking, snippets, and index freshness.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Web Search Engine?
blocks.text: A search engine takes a query like "best hiking boots" and returns the most relevant web pages in a fraction of a second, from an index of billions of documents built from a web crawl.

items: Users should be able to enter a text query and receive a ranked list of results with titles and snippets.
Newly crawled or updated pages should become searchable.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Index tens of billions of pages.
Fresh: important pages updated within hours, the long tail within days.
**Document**: a crawled page with URL, title, text, links and quality signals.
**Posting list**: for each term, the documents containing it (with positions and frequencies).
**Index shard**: a slice of the index covering a subset of documents.

blocks.code: GET /search?q=best+hiking+boots&page=1 -> { results: [{ url, title, snippet }], nextPage }

blocks.text: An **indexing pipeline** consumes crawled pages: parse HTML, extract text, tokenise and normalise (lowercase, stemming), and build an **inverted index** mapping each term to a posting list of document IDs. Link analysis (PageRank) and quality signals are computed in batch and stored per document.

The index is **sharded by document**: each leaf server holds a complete inverted index for its slice of documents. A query is sent to all shards in parallel (**scatter-gather**); each leaf finds matching documents, scores them, and returns its top results; the root merges them into the global top 10, then fetches snippets.
A large base index is rebuilt periodically, while a small **real-time index** absorbs fresh and updated pages continuously. Queries search both and merge results.
1) How should the index be partitioned?

approach.text: Each shard holds the full posting lists for a subset of terms.

challenges.text: Multi-word queries must combine posting lists across shards over the network, and popular terms create hot shards.

approach.text: Each shard indexes a subset of documents fully, so every query is answered locally per shard and merged at the root. Replicate each shard many times for query throughput, and add layers of aggregators to fan out to thousands of shards.

challenges.text: Every query touches every shard, so tail latency of the slowest shard matters — use hedged requests and timeouts that return partial results.

blocks.text: Ranking happens in stages: a fast score on each leaf (BM25 text relevance + static quality like PageRank) selects candidates, then a more expensive machine-learned ranker re-scores the merged top few hundred using many features (term proximity, freshness, click signals). Tiered indexes keep high-quality pages in a smaller tier searched first, so most queries never need the full index.
3) How do we keep latency low?

Cache results for popular queries (a large share of traffic repeats), compress posting lists (delta + variable-length encoding) so they fit in memory, early-terminate scoring once enough high-quality matches are found, and use hedged requests to cut tail latency.

quiz.question: What does an inverted index map?
options: Each term to the documents containing it
quiz.explanation: Posting lists let queries find matching documents directly.

quiz.question: Why shard the index by document rather than by term?
options: Each shard can fully answer a query locally; results are merged at the root
quiz.explanation: Term sharding requires cross-shard posting-list joins.

quiz.question: What makes freshly crawled pages searchable quickly?
options: Rebuilding the whole index every minute
A small real-time index merged with the base index at query time
quiz.explanation: The real-time index absorbs updates between base rebuilds.

quiz.question: Why use hedged requests in scatter-gather?
options: Sending a duplicate request to another replica cuts tail latency from slow shards
quiz.explanation: The slowest shard determines query latency without hedging.
